message.content:
The Battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815) was one of the bloodiest single-day engagements of the Napoleonic Wars.  While exact figures vary depending on the source, most historians agree on the following rough totals:

| Side | Killed | Wounded | Missing/Prisoners | Total |
|------|--------|---------|-------------------|-------|
| **French & allied (Bourbon & German)** | ~12 000–13 000 | ~10 000–11 000 | ~2 000–3 000 | **~25 000–27 000** |
| **Allied (British, Dutch‑Belgian, Prussian, Hanoverian, etc.)** | ~8 000–9 000 | ~7 000–8 000 | ~1 500–2 000 | **~16 000–19 000** |
| **Combined** | ~20 000–22 000 | ~17 000–19 000 | ~3 500–5 000 | **~40 000–46 000** |

**Key points**

* The French army suffered roughly 25 000 casualties (killed, wounded, missing).  
* The Allied coalition (primarily British, Dutch‑Belgian, Prussian, and Hanoverian forces) incurred about 16 000–19 000 casualties.  
* Combined casualties are therefore estimated at around 40 000–46 000 men.

These figures are derived from contemporary reports, battlefield accounts, and modern scholarly estimates. Exact numbers are difficult to pin down because record‑keeping was imperfect, many wounded were later evacuated, and some soldiers were unaccounted for after the battle. Nonetheless, the casualty totals above give a reliable sense of the scale of loss at Waterloo.
